full_title: MARILOU CASAS USAMA, COMPLAINANT, VS. (RET.) HON. OSCAR D. TOMARONG, BRANCH 28, REGIONAL TRIAL COURT, LILOY, ZAMBOANGA DEL NORTE, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. RTJ-21-017 [Formerly OCA IPI No. 19-4935-RTJ]
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Granting bail without notice to the prosecutor and without hearing: gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct
Habeas corpus is not the vehicle for granting bail; no relief for non-parties
Tallado v. Racoma outright-dismissal rule inapplicable when the complainant has no judicial remedy
Revised Rule 140: retroactivity, penalties for multiple offenses, and fine in lieu of suspension for a retired judge

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > M. Rights of the Accused

doctrine:
**In all cases, whether bail is a matter of right or of discretion, the judge must notify the prosecutor of the bail application or require his recommendation. Where bail is discretionary (offenses punishable by death, reclusion perpetua, or life imprisonment), the judge must hold a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong** (Const., Art. III, Sec. 13; Rule 114, Secs. 7, 8, and 18; OCA v. Judge Flor, Jr.; Villanueva v. Judge Buaya, which requires notice and hearing even when bail is a matter of right, to apply the Section 9 guidelines in fixing the amount). The judge's own view that the killing was "only homicide," and the fact that no Information had yet been filed, do not excuse notice and hearing. A judge who grants bail on the day it is filed without either commits **gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct**. A petition for habeas corpus is not the proper vehicle to assert a right to bail (Galvez v. CA), and ordering the release on bail of persons who are not parties to the habeas corpus case is a separate act of gross ignorance and gross misconduct.

The rule in Tallado v. Racoma (an administrative complaint is dismissed outright if a judicial remedy is still available) does not apply where the complainant had no judicial remedy. A private offended party, whose interest is limited to the civil aspect, has no legal personality to question a grant of bail.

The Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, effective April 4, 2022) applies to all pending and future cases even if prejudicial to the respondent (Sec. 24), and Dela Rama v. De Leon is abandoned. Under Section 21, separate acts are penalized separately, while a single act constituting several offenses gets only the penalty for the most serious. **When a respondent who deserves suspension can no longer serve it because of retirement, the Court applies Section 18(b) by analogy and imposes a fine under Section 17(1)(c).** The Court will no longer impose "forfeiture of salary" equivalent to the suspension period, a practice derived from the civil service rules.
facts:
On May 4, 2016, days before the May 9, 2016 elections, police officers on patrol in Tampilisan, Zamboanga del Norte exchanged gunfire with mayoral candidate Alson Chan and his campaign volunteers. PO1 Mirdan Usama, complainant's husband, was killed. Chan and his volunteers were arrested on the morning of May 5, 2016.

At 2:00 p.m. on May 5, 2016, a Muslim holiday, Chan filed with respondent Judge Tomarong's court (RTC Branch 28, Liloy) an "Application to Post Bail and to Release the Detained Person Pending Filing of Proper Information" (Misc. Sp. Proc. No. MSP-328). The application stated that an Information would be filed on May 6. The same day, respondent granted bail at P200,000.00. He did not notify the prosecutor and held no hearing. The police refused to release Chan. On May 6, after inquest, the provincial prosecutor prepared Informations against Chan and three volunteers for murder, two counts of attempted murder, illegal possession of firearms (RA 10591), and illegal possession of explosives (RA 9616).

On May 7, Chan's wife filed a petition for habeas corpus for Chan only (Sp. Proc. No. SR-763). Respondent issued the writ, and after a hearing on May 10 he ordered "the release of accused Alson Chan and the released (sic) of the three other accused ... after posting a bail of ... (P200,000.00) each in all cases that will be filed against them." Complainant moved for his inhibition the same day, and respondent inhibited on July 26, 2016.

Complainant filed her Complaint-Affidavit dated February 19, 2019. Respondent optionally retired effective April 1, 2019. In his Comment, he invoked SC Circular No. 95-96 on acting on bail during weekends and holidays. He said he had "analyzed" that the crime was only homicide, a bailable offense, so no hearing was needed, and that his acts were judicial in nature. The JIB found him liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. It recommended forfeiture of one year's salary and benefits, in lieu of one year's suspension, with a stern warning.
issues: Whether the administrative complaint should be dismissed outright under Tallado v. Racoma because a judicial remedy was available to the complainant.
Whether respondent is administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.
What penalty should be imposed on respondent, considering his retirement.
ruling:
**1. No.** Tallado laid down guidelines against abuse of the administrative disciplinary mechanism, including outright dismissal when a judicial remedy is still available. That rule does not apply here because complainant had no judicial remedy against the grant of bail. In criminal cases the State is the real party in interest, and the private offended party's interest is limited to civil liability. **As the victim's widow, complainant had no legal personality to question the grant of bail**, so the Court proceeded to the merits.

**2. Yes, on two separate acts.** The Court applied the Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC). Section 24 makes it retroactive to all pending cases even if prejudicial, so it is "uniformly applicable to all cases, regardless of when the infractions are committed." Chan was charged with murder, punishable by reclusion perpetua to death, so bail was discretionary and required a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt was strong (Rule 114, Secs. 7 and 8). Notice to the prosecutor is required in all cases (Rule 114, Sec. 18; OCA v. Judge Flor, Jr.). The absence of an Information on May 5 did not excuse notice and hearing, especially since Chan's own application said one would be filed the next day and respondent knew the detention involved a killing. His "appreciation" that the crime was only homicide "cannot do away with the requirement of conducting a hearing." **Granting bail on the same day without notice and hearing was gross ignorance of the law, and his flagrant disregard of the rules on bail was gross misconduct.**

Second, in the habeas corpus case he ordered the release on bail of the three volunteers, who were not parties to it, which was a separate act of gross ignorance. He also disregarded the scope of habeas corpus under Rule 102, Section 1: "a petition for habeas corpus is not the appropriate vehicle for asserting a right to bail or vindicating its denial" (Galvez v. CA). That flagrant disregard was also gross misconduct.

**3. A fine of P110,000.00 per act, or P220,000.00 in total.** Gross ignorance and gross misconduct are serious charges (Sec. 17(1)). Under Section 21, each act constituting both offenses gets one penalty, and the two separate acts get separate penalties. The Court found one year's suspension commensurate for each act (Sec. 17(1)(b)), but respondent had retired. The JIB's recommended forfeiture of one year's salary is a civil-service practice that the Court "should no longer perpetuate." Section 18 covers only respondents who deserve dismissal, but **the Court applied Section 18(b) by analogy and imposed a fine within the range of Section 17(1)(c) (more than P100,000.00 up to P200,000.00) in lieu of suspension.** A stern warning is no longer viable for a retired judge.
disposition: Retired Judge Oscar D. Tomarong was found GUILTY of two counts of gross ignorance of the law and two counts of gross misconduct arising from two separate acts. He would have been suspended for one year without salary and benefits for each act had he not retired on April 1, 2019. He was ordered to pay a FINE of P110,000.00 for each act, or P220,000.00 in total, within three months from promulgation. If unpaid, the amount will be deducted from his retirement benefits, including his accrued leave credits.

bar_questions.q: Diego was arrested without a warrant for shooting a barangay tanod to death. That same afternoon, before any Information was filed, Diego applied for bail with the RTC, stating that an Information would be filed the next day. Judge Rivera granted bail of P150,000.00 within an hour. He did not notify the prosecutor and held no hearing because, in his view, the killing was only homicide. The next day, an Information for murder was filed. (a) Is Judge Rivera administratively liable? (b) If Judge Rivera has since retired and the Court finds that his offense merits one year's suspension, what penalty may be imposed?

alac.answer: (a) Yes. Judge Rivera is liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. (b) A fine under Section 17(1)(c) of the Revised Rule 140, applying Section 18(b) by analogy, not forfeiture of one year's salary.
alac.legal_basis: Whether bail is a matter of right or discretion, the judge must notify the prosecutor or require his recommendation. Where the offense is punishable by reclusion perpetua, he must hold a hearing to determine whether the evidence of guilt is strong (Rule 114, Secs. 7, 8, and 18). Patent disregard of these elementary rules is gross ignorance of the law, and flagrant disregard of them is gross misconduct. When a respondent who deserves suspension can no longer serve it because of retirement, the Court imposes a fine under Section 17(1)(c), applying Section 18(b) by analogy. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
alac.application: Diego was detained for a killing and was about to be charged, so a bail hearing and notice to the prosecutor were necessary. That no Information had yet been filed did not excuse them. The judge's private estimate that the crime was only homicide cannot replace the hearing, whose necessity depends on the gravity of the offense charged, here murder. Granting bail within an hour without notice and hearing shows a disregard of basic rules. Since Judge Rivera has retired, suspension can no longer be served. Following Usama, the Court imposes a fine of more than P100,000.00 up to P200,000.00, not the civil-service practice of forfeiting salary equivalent to the suspension period.
alac.conclusion: Judge Rivera is liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct, and being retired, he may be fined under Section 17(1)(c) of the Revised Rule 140 in lieu of suspension.

bar_questions.q: The widow of the slain tanod filed an administrative complaint against Judge Rivera for granting bail to Diego without notice and hearing. Judge Rivera moves to dismiss the complaint outright under Tallado v. Racoma, arguing that the widow should first have questioned the bail order in a judicial action, such as certiorari. Should the complaint be dismissed outright?

alac.answer: No. The outright-dismissal rule in Tallado does not apply because the widow had no judicial remedy against the grant of bail.
alac.legal_basis: Under Tallado v. Racoma, an administrative complaint is dismissed outright if a judicial remedy is still available to the complainant. In criminal cases, however, the State is the real party in interest, and the private offended party's interest is limited to the civil liability. A private offended party therefore has no legal personality to question the grant of bail, so Tallado's rule does not apply. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
alac.application: The widow is only a private offended party in the criminal case against Diego. She cannot assail the bail order on her own because only the State, through the prosecutor, may do so. Since no judicial remedy was available to her, there is nothing she must first exhaust, and her administrative complaint may proceed on the merits.
alac.conclusion: The motion to dismiss should be denied, and the administrative complaint resolved on the merits.

bar_questions.q: Lorna filed a petition for habeas corpus for her husband Andres, who had been detained since his warrantless arrest for a stabbing. At the hearing, the prosecutor manifested that an Information would be filed that day. Judge Cruz then ordered the release of Andres and of two co-detainees, Ben and Carlo, "upon posting bail of P100,000.00 each in all cases that will be filed against them." Ben and Carlo were not named in the petition. Did Judge Cruz act properly?

alac.answer: No. Judge Cruz misused the habeas corpus proceeding to grant bail and granted relief to non-parties. This is gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 102, Section 1, the writ of habeas corpus extends to cases of illegal confinement or detention; its purpose is to inquire into involuntary restraint and to relieve a person from it if illegal. A petition for habeas corpus is not the appropriate vehicle for asserting a right to bail or vindicating its denial (Galvez v. CA). Ordering in a habeas corpus case the release on bail of persons who are not parties to it is gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct. (Usama v. Judge Tomarong, A.M. No. RTJ-21-017, March 8, 2023, En Banc)
alac.application: The only question in Lorna's petition was whether Andres's detention was illegal. Instead of resolving that question, Judge Cruz fixed bail, which belongs to the bail rules under Rule 114 with notice to the prosecutor and a hearing where required. He also extended the relief to Ben and Carlo, who had not sought any relief from the court and were not parties. Both acts show a flagrant disregard of the rules on habeas corpus and bail.
alac.conclusion: Judge Cruz acted improperly and may be held administratively liable for gross ignorance of the law and gross misconduct.

notes: Decided under the Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, 2022). The 2027 syllabus bases Judicial Ethics on the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC); check whether that Code changed the sanctions and section numbers cited here. The complaint was filed on February 19, 2019, before respondent's optional retirement took effect on April 1, 2019; the decision did not separately discuss jurisdiction over a retired judge. Marquez, J. took no part because of prior action as Court Administrator.
